body:
Claude: **suggestion**: The bulk fast path drops the "read until NUL, at most `length` bytes" tolerance the old per-character walk had, and turns an over-stated `length` into an out-of-bounds read.

Previously every iteration went through `utf8_encoded_valid_unichar(p, length)`, which never reads past the first NUL: `utf8_encoded_expected_len(0)` returns 1 and `unichar_is_control(0)` is true, so the function returned false at the NUL without ever touching anything beyond it. That made `utf8_is_printable_newline(str, SIZE_MAX, ...)` safe on a NUL-terminated buffer - and `SIZE_MAX` is explicitly documented as a legal length by `utf8_encoded_valid_unichar_full()` right below in this same file, as well as by `utf8_is_valid_n()` and `ascii_is_valid_n()` in the same header. With the word scan, `n == sizeof(uint64_t)` for any `length >= 8`, so this `unaligned_read_ne64(p)` pulls in eight bytes before anything looks at their values. A NUL inside the word does make `is_printable_fastpath_u64()` fail and the function still returns false, but only after the load has already happened.

Reproduced independently by two reviewers: a 4-byte heap allocation holding `"abc\0"` scanned with `length == SIZE_MAX` gives an ASan `heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 8, 0 bytes after 4-byte region`, where the pre-change code returned false cleanly.

Nothing in tree is affected today - logs-show.c, sd-dhcp-client-id.c, journal-upload-journal.c and utf8.c:265 all pass exact byte counts - so this is latent. It is still worth closing, because `SIZE_MAX` is the established "unbounded/NUL-terminated" idiom for the neighbouring functions declared in this very header, one of which this same commit touches, so a future caller reaching for it here would get a heap over-read rather than an error. Either reject it up front with `assert(length != SIZE_MAX)`, or keep the old semantics by taking the eight-byte load only when `length != SIZE_MAX && length >= sizeof(uint64_t)`.

For exact lengths the bounds are tight: ~40M differentially fuzzed inputs on exact-size heap buffers and flush against a `PROT_NONE` guard page produced zero over-reads and zero behavioural divergences from the base implementation.
